title: DeepSeek R1 vs V3 for Workflow Automation (2026)
summary: V3 responds immediately while R1 reasons through problems. Determine which model reduces execution time while handling your task complexity.
body_markdown:
## Run either DeepSeek model with Activepieces


Point any step at either DeepSeek model and change that choice later without rebuilding the flow:[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/deepseek-r1-vs-v3-for-business-ai-2026-guide) allows unlimited flows on every plan, including free, so a V3 version and an R1 version of the same flow can sit side by side for the comparison above.


It's an automation builder where each workflow step is a block on a canvas. It connects to DeepSeek through an API connection or a plain HTTP request step.


A self-hosted DeepSeek deployment or a different provider works the same way, because the step only needs an endpoint and a model name.


### Route workflow steps between DeepSeek V3 and R1


Send routine steps such as extraction, classification and drafting to V3, and only the steps that need multi-step reasoning to R1.


A platform that sells you its own bundled model has settled V3 versus R1 for you, and set the price, before you build anything; Activepieces sells no model, so it calls whichever DeepSeek you picked on your own provider key, the spend lands on your provider account at your rate, and you can reach it from Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client.


Bring-your-own-key starts on the Plus plan at $20 a month, so accessing it requires a Plus subscription.


That keeps the call on each step yours. With your own key, every AI step is 1 credit, while R1's reasoning tokens are billed by your provider, so the credit count stays flat and the R1 cost follows your vendor's rate.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


A useful pattern is to let V3 attempt the step first and escalate when its result looks weak.


If the extracted fields are incomplete or the model reports low confidence, a condition sends that run to R1 for a second pass. The cheaper model handles the bulk, and the expensive one sees only the exceptions.


Because the model is a setting on a single step, swapping V3 for R1, or for another provider, means editing that setting. The branches and conditions around it stay as they are.


### Add human approval and fallbacks to workflows


In the screenshot below, a six-step document workflow puts this into practice. A web form collects the input, an extraction step turns the document into structured data, and a to-do creates a human approval.


Once the answer comes back, a status check branches on it: accepted runs create the customer record in Stripe, the payments platform, while rejected runs send an email through Gmail.


Nothing irreversible happens until a person has said yes, and the decision is recorded on the to-do.


In your own flow, the extraction step is where V3 or R1 would sit, and the rejected branch is your fallback. A rejection can send the run back for an R1 retry or hand it to a person, rather than ending silently.


**Place the approval before every step you can't reverse, and the model choice upstream becomes a cost decision instead of a risk decision.**
